title: About me
text: I am an early-career ecologist driven by questions about how species interact and how those interactions shape ecological communities. I graduated from Colorado College in May 2025 with distinction in Organismal Biology and Ecology, along with 2 minors in Environmental Studies and Race, Ethnicity, and Migration Studies. My positionality as a queer woman of color in STEM and through my academic background at the intersection of science and race studies, means I approach ecology with a deep awareness of how knowledge is shaped by who is included, heard, and supported. I believe that science, and the communities it serves, are strongest when informed by diverse lived experiences and perspectives, a value that guides both my research path and my commitment to collaborative, inclusive scientific spaces. I currently work in the tropics at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) as a Global Sustainability Scholar and RaMP-UP Research Fellow. My research focuses on termite ecology and behavior, with an emphasis on predator–prey dynamics and how these relationships influence colony defense investments and carbon cycling.

title: Emily Marple
text: Hi! I’m Emily (she/her). I am an early-career ecologist drawn to questions about how species interact and how those interactions shape ecological communities. My research interests are broad, ranging in ecosystems and study species. Think lakes, deserts, birds, bees, butterflies, and now termites :) Outside of work, you can find me dancing, hiking, running, and learning how to play guitar. I love to move and create!

title: How much is a queen worth?
text:
Whack. Whack. Whack.
“Que estás haciendo?” Pregunta el janitor.
I look up at the shadow standing over me, backlit by the sun. “Oh! Um. Hola. Es un nido de las termitas. Matarlos en el… freezer? Y ahora yo necesito… um… mezclarlos? Porque necesito saber cuantos son?” I stutter in broken Spanish.
Does what I’m doing make sense in any language?
I’m kneeling outside of the loading dock on a tarp, holding a bright yellow hammer, dripping sweat as the sun beats down, relentless in this constant summer heat and humidity. Fragments of termite bodies and pieces of the nest are splattered down my shirt and in my hair.
Thankfully, he accepts my answer with a “Que cool!” and heads inside. I continue my hammering. Termite nests are surprisingly sturdy overall. The outside falls away easily, crumbling in my fingers. But as you get closer to the center, the nest thickens and hardens. It soon just becomes beating what feels like an unshapely log apart, as the nests are made of semi digested wood and termite spit.
Whack. Another chunk breaks off. I can feel her presence. I can feel that I’m close. I raise my arms high and slam the last bit in half. I pick up the fragments and sort through the dust carefully. There she is. The queen.
Termite queens are the longest living insects in the entire world. They live to at least 25 years. Some species make it to 50. And it’s possible that they could live up to 100 years— no one has stuck around to check. Stuck in this essentially impenetrable maze— I will never expect to monitor one alive in natural conditions. It would require precision and resources that I simply don’t have access to.
I roll her gently in my fingers, inspecting her tiny head. Her white, pudgy body envelops her. It’s as if you stuck a tiny ant head on a maggot’s body. The queens don’t walk or move around much. They are egg laying machines, producing hundreds a day. They have to be fed and groomed by the workers, and are fiercely protected by the soldiers. Both get nothing in return. They live, work, and die for her. Evolved over thousands of years as a super organism that functions in perfect cohesion.
And now she’s dead. Home ripped off a tree branch, frozen in a -4 degree celsius freezer (walk-in, state of the art by the way), smashed apart by a 22 year old girl with a brand new hammer. I sigh. 25, 50 years? 100? I haven’t even made it to 23 yet, and I feel like I’ve lived several lifetimes. All of this just so I can attempt to satiate the human desire to learn more about this place we call home— as if we’ll ever be able to fully understand the complexities of our existence and the world around us. All this so I can count the corpses of her family, her children, pick them out of their carefully built home and then toss them right in the trash after.
Once I take the nest fragments I need inside (thoroughly mixing them and measuring 50 grams) I begin the laborious task of counting. I shine a light on the tiny soldiers and workers, using tweezers to pluck them out of the crevices of the nest. They huddle together. I think of them huddling in the cold of the freezer. I hope it was peaceful. I hope they weren’t scared. Shut up, Emily. They are just termites, and you signed up for this job. But I can’t help it. I can’t help but feel for these little creatures. It simultaneously makes me feel better and worse to observe them when they are alive. They are so cute. The soldiers look frantically around, wiggling their pointy noses (or nasuses, mind you) looking for the source of the danger. So brave! I am also burdened with the new knowledge that the older soldiers (these guys have a lifespan of 1-2 years, unless a pesky human decided to steal and freeze them) volunteer for the riskier jobs near the surface of the nest, allowing younger soldiers to work the safer jobs, like protecting the queen in the already fortified queens chamber. Do you think termites can feel love?
I had a mentor tell me once, “If you like bugs, don’t become an entomologist. All you do is kill them.” I laughed at the time. I understand now.
So here I am. Stuck between a rock and a hard place, in my self-imposed moral dilemma. But who cares, really? There’s millions of termites out there. But it matters to that one, doesn’t it? I can’t erase the voice in the back of my head. She’s screaming, actually. But isn’t this science?
I can only move forward by reminding myself that first of all, I need to stop anthropomorphizing critters, no matter how tempting. And second of all, conducting research that helps us understand the role of termites in our ecosystem helps them all in the long run. From my time here, I’ve grown to love these pesky, painful, and abundant insects, and I wish that other people knew they do more than destroy houses. And I hope that from my research I can help destigmatize them, and demonstrate that these guys who enjoy eating wood actually have an incredibly important function in carbon cycling and decomposition.
Anyways, this is a slightly dramatic take on how I feel about my work. I will likely continue to have various moral dilemmas as I continue in this field (as a self-proclaimed empath!!!), but continue because I know understanding our ecosystems is the first step in protecting them.
With abundant love, Emily
